planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and leave uncovered since light aids germination; unlike common foxglove this sterile hybrid is a true, reliably perennial clump that returns for several years instead of dying after its second season.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in part shade, where its unusual coppery rose-pink spikes stand out against the more common purples and whites of other foxgloves. Because it is a hybrid between Digitalis purpurea and D. grandiflora, it sets little viable seed and is usually propagated instead by division of established clumps in spring or fall. Deadhead the central spike after bloom to encourage smaller secondary flower spikes later in the season. All plant parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Start seed indoors on the surface of moist mix 6-8 weeks before last frost, as light aids germination; plants form a rosette the first year and bloom the second, behaving as a short-lived perennial in favorable sites.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; the narrower, densely felted gray-green leaves and slender spikes of tubular, netted-veined cream-and-tan flowers give this species a more refined, subtle look than common foxglove. It is the primary commercial source of the cardiac glycoside digoxin and should never be handled without care, as all parts are highly toxic if ingested. Cut back spent flower spikes to tidy the planting, and expect self-sown seedlings to appear in following years.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; established clumps resent disturbance so choose a permanent site.

directions: A vigorous, long-blooming selection bearing semi-double white flowers with a faint greenish reverse on the outer petals, held on branching stems well above fig-shaped basal foliage from late summer into fall. It is slower to establish than the species but eventually spreads by shallow rhizomes to form a substantial colony, making it valuable for filling gaps in the fading late-season shade border. Leave the finely cut seed heads standing for autumn texture, and mulch in colder zones to protect the crown over winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; give it room, as this is one of the larger-growing Japanese anemone selections.

directions: This robust, tall-growing cultivar produces large, semi-double, clear pink flowers with a ring of golden stamens on sturdy branching stems from late summer through fall. Its extra height makes it a good back-of-border companion for shorter fall bloomers, and the coarse, dark green foliage stays attractive all season. Once established it spreads readily by underground stems, so site it where a colony is welcome rather than in a tightly bordered bed.

common_name: Prinz Heinrich Japanese Anemone (Prince Henry Anemone)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this older, well-tested German selection is a reliable choice for cooler-summer gardens.

directions: A classic, compact-growing cultivar with semi-double, deep rose-pink flowers held on branching stems from late summer into fall, more contained in habit than many later Japanese anemone introductions. The dark, fig-like foliage forms a tidy mound through summer, and the plant spreads modestly by rhizome once settled in. It combines well with earlier-blooming perennials whose foliage it can screen once they finish flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; its compact stature suits smaller borders where taller anemone cultivars would overwhelm.

directions: A German-bred dwarf selection carrying fully double, rich rose-pink flowers with a neatly ruffled center on relatively short, sturdy stems, making it one of the more compact Japanese anemones suited to front-of-border placement. It blooms over a long late-summer-to-fall window and holds up well without staking. Provide consistent moisture during dry spells, since shallow-rooted anemones wilt quickly in drought.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full shade; this white-flowered sport is slightly less vigorous than the species and benefits from a touch more shade in hot climates to keep the foliage from bleaching.

directions: A clumping, non-running lilyturf selection valued for its clean white flower spikes held above grass-like, glossy dark-green foliage in mid-to-late summer, followed by black berries into fall. It combines well as a pale edging accent among the more common purple-flowered forms of Liriope muscari and stays evergreen in mild climates. Shear back tattered winter foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to keep clumps tidy.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold stratify seed 8-10 weeks at 35-40F before spring sowing; established plants may also be propagated by division. Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Unlike the shorter, more rounded flowers of European globeflower, this taller Chinese species opens into flatter, more open cups of vivid orange-gold with a prominent central boss of narrow petaloid stamens, borne well above deeply cut, dark green foliage in early summer. It thrives at the moist edge of a pond or stream and struggles in dry soil or summer heat, performing best in cooler regions. Deadhead spent flowers to tidy the clump, and divide every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Oscar Schoaf Rue Anemone (Double Pink Rue Anemone)

planting.note: Plant tuberous divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; this double-flowered selection is slower to spread than the wild species and is best left undisturbed once sited.

directions: This heirloom double-flowered form produces small, fully double, soft pink pompon blooms held above whorls of delicate, blue-green foliage in early spring, resembling tiny rosebuds rather than the simple starry flowers of the wild rue anemone. Because it sets no viable seed, propagation is strictly by division of its small tuberous roots after the foliage yellows in early summer. Plant it among ferns or hostas that will fill the space once it goes fully dormant for the season.

common_name: Betty Blake Rue Anemone (Double White Rue Anemone)

planting.note: Plant tuberous divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; give it a permanent, undisturbed spot alongside other spring ephemerals.

directions: A charming double-flowered white counterpart to the pink double rue anemone selections, opening tight, camellia-like pompon blooms over finely divided, blue-green foliage in early to mid spring. Like other double forms it is sterile and spreads only slowly from its cluster of tuberous roots, so patience is required to build a sizeable patch. The foliage disappears by early summer, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant roots.
